metaData.title: Maintainability sensors for coding agents
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores how static code analysis sensors, enhanced with custom guidance for AI coding agents, can help maintain codebase maintainability by providing fast feedback and enabling agent self-correction.
metaData.summary: Martin Fowler discusses the challenge of maintaining codebase maintainability when using AI coding agents, drawing from his experience rebuilding an internal analytics dashboard with AI. He defines maintainability as making it easy and low-risk to change code over time, noting that AI agents face similar issues as human developers in tangled codebases. The article focuses on using 'sensors'—tools that provide feedback to agents for self-correction. The primary sensor explored is ESLint, configured with custom rules targeting common AI failure modes like excessive function arguments, file length, and cyclomatic complexity. A key innovation is the use of custom ESLint formatters that provide guidance text, instructing the agent on how to handle warnings (e.g., making judgment calls on type suppression, or slightly increasing thresholds as a last resort). Fowler observes that AI frequently increased the cyclomatic complexity threshold, suggesting the guidance text was effective. He notes that managing warnings becomes more feasible with AI, as agents can handle the tedious task of suppression. The article concludes that the cost-benefit balance of static analysis has shifted: AI reduces the cost of creating custom rules, and the benefit increases by catching common AI mistakes. However, he warns against a false sense of security, as static analysis cannot catch semantic quality issues, and there is a risk of feedback overload leading to over-engineering.

mainPoints.point: Static code analysis sensors, enhanced with custom guidance, can effectively help AI coding agents self-correct and maintain codebase maintainability.
mainPoints.explanation: By configuring tools like ESLint with rules targeting common AI failure modes (e.g., function length, cyclomatic complexity) and providing custom guidance messages, agents receive fast, actionable feedback to improve code quality during development.

mainPoints.point: Custom guidance for self-correction is a powerful form of prompt injection that improves agent behavior.
mainPoints.explanation: Instead of just flagging an error, the guidance text instructs the agent on how to handle the warning, such as making a judgment call on type suppression or slightly increasing a threshold as a last resort, leading to more nuanced and appropriate corrections.

mainPoints.point: AI agents make managing static analysis warnings more feasible by handling the tedious task of suppression and threshold adjustments.
mainPoints.explanation: The cost-benefit balance of static analysis has shifted: AI reduces the cost of creating custom rules and managing warnings, while the benefit increases by catching common AI mistakes that human developers might not make as frequently.

mainPoints.point: There is a risk of a false sense of security and feedback overload when relying on static analysis for quality.
mainPoints.explanation: Static analysis cannot catch semantic quality issues, and activating too many rules can overwhelm the agent with feedback, potentially leading to over-engineered refactorings or an illusion of quality.

keyQuotes: A sensor is meant to give the agent feedback so that it can self-correct. Ideally, we want to give the agent extra context for that self-correction - a good kind of prompt injection.
With coding agents, we might now have a chance at that clean baseline.

Cost is reduced because it's much cheaper to create custom scripts and rules with AI. And the benefit has also increased: the analysis results help me get a first sense of lots of hygiene factors that wouldn't even happen that much when I write code myself.
I can't help but wonder if this can also lead to a false sense of security and an illusion of quality.
I worry about feedback overload for the agent, sending it into a spiral of over-engineered refactorings.

relatedArticles.title: Design-First Collaboration
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Martin Fowler introduces a 'Design-First' framework for AI collaboration, advocating for a structured, five-level sequential dialogue to prevent the 'Implementation Trap' and ensure architectural alignment before generating code.

relatedArticles.title: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents， AutoResearch， and the Loopy Era of AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Andrej Karpathy explores the paradigm shift from manual programming to agent orchestration, the automation of AI research, and the profound implications for software engineering and education.

relatedArticles.title: Building Claude Code with Boris Cherny
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, discusses his 100% AI-driven workflow, Anthropic's unique engineering culture, and why software engineers are transitioning from 'scribes' to 'authors' in the AI era.

relatedArticles.title: What Is Code?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Code is not just instructions for machines but a conceptual model of a problem domain, and as LLMs commoditize code generation, building precise vocabulary and shared understanding becomes the developer's core value.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering for coding agent users
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Martin Fowler defines 'harness engineering' as the systematic practice of building feedforward guides and feedback sensors to steer AI coding agents toward maintainable, architecturally fit, and functionally correct code.

relatedArticles.title: Structured-Prompt-Driven Development (SPDD)
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Structured Prompt-Driven Development (SPDD) is an engineering method that treats prompts as first-class delivery artifacts, enabling teams to govern, review, and reuse AI-generated code at scale.

relatedArticles.title: Harness design for long-running application development
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores Anthropic's multi-agent harness design (Planner, Generator, Evaluator) for long-running autonomous coding, detailing how to overcome context anxiety and self-evaluation bias to build complex full-stack applications.

relatedArticles.title: How Claude Code works in large codebases: Best practices and where to start | Claude
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a comprehensive guide on deploying Claude Code in large codebases, emphasizing that success depends more on the 'harness' of configuration layers (CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins, LSP, MCP) than on the model alone, and outlines proven patterns for making codebases navigable, maintaining configurations, and assigning organizational ownership.

relatedArticles.title: Martin Fowler & Kent Beck: Frameworks for reinventing software， again and again
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Software legends Martin Fowler and Kent Beck discuss how AI redefines software engineering, emphasizing that core practices like TDD and modularity remain essential for human-AI collaboration.

relatedArticles.title: Humans and Agents in Software Engineering Loops
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Martin Fowler proposes a 'human-on-the-loop' framework where developers focus on 'Harness Engineering'—designing the systems and constraints that guide AI agents—rather than micromanaging code or abandoning oversight.
